cards.text: Micah, a prophet of the LORD, has a message, and he aims it right at the top. The prophet says, 'Hear now, O leaders of Jacob, you rulers of the house of Israel.' Then he asks them a question.

cards.question: Micah asks the leaders of Jacob and the rulers of Israel a question. Of all people, shouldn't they know ___?
The leaders of Jacob should know justice. Micah says they love good and hate evil.

cards.text: Nope, flip it. Micah says they hate good and love evil: 'You tear the skin from my people and strip the flesh from their bones.'

cards.question: Micah keeps that rough picture going. He says the leaders of Jacob chop up the people like what?

cards.text: Then Micah says a time is coming when these same leaders will cry out to the LORD.

cards.question: The leaders of Jacob cry out to the LORD. What happens?

answers.text: He sends them a new king

cards.question: Micah says the LORD will hide His face from these leaders because of the evil they have done.

cards.text: Now the LORD speaks about the prophets who lead His people astray. These prophets proclaim peace while they chew with their teeth.

cards.question: These prophets proclaim peace while they chew. But against someone who puts nothing in their mouths, they declare ___.

cards.text: So the LORD says night will come over these prophets without visions, and the daylight will turn black over them. Signal from heaven? ZERO bars.

cards.question: Once the visions are gone, the seers and diviners are honored for their honesty.
The seers and diviners all end up covering their mouths. Why?

answers.text: There is no answer from God
The leaders ordered them to be quiet
They are afraid of the angry crowds

cards.text: Then the prophet Micah says, 'As for me, however,' and the whole tone changes. Those prophets got no answer from God, but Micah has something they don't.

cards.question: Micah says he is filled with power by the ___ of the LORD.
Micah is filled with power, justice and courage. What does he declare to Jacob and Israel?

cards.text: Then Micah calls out the leaders of Jacob and rulers of Israel again. He says they despise justice and pervert all that is right.

cards.question: Micah says these leaders build Zion with ___ and Jerusalem with iniquity.

cards.text: Then Micah goes down the list, and it's price tags all the way down. Jerusalem's leaders judge for a bribe, and her prophets practice divination for money.

cards.question: In Jerusalem, Micah says, the priests are the ones who teach for free.
Bribes and price tags all over Jerusalem, and yet they lean on the LORD. What do they say?

answers.text: The LORD is among us so no disaster can come
The LORD has left us so we should repent now
The LORD is angry so we must hide from Him

cards.text: Then Micah says what's coming because of them, and he starts with Zion.

cards.question: Micah tells the leaders and rulers he's calling out, 'Therefore, because of you,' and then names what happens to Zion. What is it?

answers.text: It will be plowed like a field
It will be rebuilt with gold
It will be ruled by Egypt

cards.question: Micah says that even as Jerusalem falls, the temple mount will be spared.

cards.text: Jerusalem becomes a heap of rubble, and the temple mount a wooded ridge. That's where Micah's warning lands, friend, and it does not land soft.

findings.problem: Micah 3:1 opens with 'Then I said,' so the passage starts in the middle of Micah's message. The opening card names the speaker and the audience, but it gives no context for what came before.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: Only the right answer uses the future tense, which matches the text's 'will.' 'He will not answer them' stands out from 'He answers them right away' and 'He sends them a new king.' The question is also in the present tense ('cry out... What happens?'), but verse 4 describes a future time.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: The right answer 'Spirit' is capitalized and the wrong answers 'house' and 'servants' are lowercase. The capital letter points to the right answer.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The setup line says Micah's list is 'price tags all the way down.' Card 7 then asks whether the priests teach for free. Since the priests are on that list, the setup line already rules out the wrong answer.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: Across the walkthrough, Papa Dorin has only a few light touches: 'aims it right at the top,' 'Nope, flip it,' 'ZERO bars' and 'price tags all the way down.' Most story cards are plain retellings with no reaction, disbelief or self-deprecation. Stop 2 has almost no humor, and there is little shifting between laid-back and LOUD.

rule.text: Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: Stop 2's range is Micah 3:8-12, but card 1 cites Micah 3:7-8 because it looks back at verse 7 ('Those prophets got no answer from God') to set up the contrast in verse 8. The citation follows 'cite exactly what the card uses,' so it is accurate, but it falls outside the stop's verse range.
findings.question: Can a story card cite a verse from an earlier stop's range when it refers back to that verse for contrast? Or must every card's citation stay inside its own stop's range, with the look-back worded so it cites nothing outside it?
